passages.t: A thief, and a break-in at night
passages.happening:
“If a man steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters or sells it, he must repay five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep” (verse 1).

“If a thief is caught breaking in and is beaten to death, no one shall be guilty of bloodshed” (verse 2). “But if it happens after sunrise, there is guilt for his bloodshed. A thief must make full restitution; if he has nothing, he himself shall be sold for his theft” (verse 3).

If the stolen animal is found alive in his hands, “he must pay back double” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The Book of the Covenant turns from injuries to property. Israel lived by farming and herding. Wealth was counted in flocks, herds, grain and vineyards, and there were no banks, insurers or police. So most disputes were about animals and crops.

The aim of these laws is restitution: the thief pays the owner back, and more. An ox was worth more than a sheep, and a thief who had already killed or sold the animal had gone further than one caught with it still alive, so the payment is larger. Hammurabi's law, older and harsher, could demand up to thirtyfold, and a thief who could not pay was put to death. In Israel's law a thief who has nothing is sold into service to make the loss good. He is not put to death for stealing property.

The break-in at night is a careful case. In the dark a burglar could not be seen or recognized, and he might be armed. A householder who killed him then was not guilty. After sunrise, when the thief could be seen and caught, killing him became bloodshed. Even a thief's life counted.
passages.later:
Zacchaeus, the tax collector, reached for this law when he met Jesus: “if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold” (Luke 19:8).

Paul gives the thief a new way to live: “He who has been stealing must steal no longer, but must work, doing good with his own hands, that he may have something to share with the one in need” (Ephesians 4:28).
passages.asks: The law asks the thief to put things right, not only to be sorry. Ask whether there is something you have taken, money, time, credit or trust, that you need to give back. And ask what full restitution would look like.

passages.t: Fields, fire, and things held in trust
passages.happening:
If someone lets his animals graze in another man's field, “he must make restitution from the best of his own field or vineyard” (verse 5). If someone starts a fire that spreads to a neighbor's grain, “the one who started the fire must make full restitution” (verse 6).

If goods left with a neighbor are stolen and the thief is not found, the neighbor must appear before the judges (verses 7-8). In a dispute over who owns something, “both parties shall bring their cases before the judges” (verse 9).

If an animal left in a neighbor's care dies or is lost “while no one is watching”, the neighbor swears an oath before the LORD, and the owner accepts it (verses 10-11). An animal torn by a wild beast is brought as evidence (verse 13). A borrowed animal that dies must be paid for, unless the owner was there, or it was hired (verses 14-15).
passages.hearers:
Neighbors in a village depended on one another. They left animals and goods in each other's keeping, borrowed oxen for plowing, and grazed flocks beside each other's fields. These laws sort out the losses that come from living that close.

They are ordered by degrees of responsibility. Carelessness that ruins a neighbor's crop must be paid for from your best. Goods stolen from your keeping lead to a hearing. An animal that dies when no one could have stopped it needs only an oath.

When there was no witness, the two sides came ‘before the judges’. The Hebrew word there is elohim, which can mean God or judges; the BSB takes it as the judges. Either way, they swore an oath and trusted God to deal with anyone who lied.

The torn carcass was proof. A shepherd who brought back what was left after a lion or wolf showed that a wild animal took it, not he.
passages.later: The prophet Amos borrowed the picture of the shepherd's evidence: “As the shepherd snatches from the mouth of the lion two legs or a piece of an ear, so the Israelites dwelling in Samaria will be rescued” (Amos 3:12). Only a remnant would be left.
passages.asks: These laws ask neighbors to care for what belongs to one another. Ask whether you treat what others have lent or trusted to you as carefully as your own. And ask whether your carelessness has cost someone else, and what you owe them.

passages.t: A man who seduces an unmarried woman
passages.happening:
“If a man seduces a virgin who is not pledged in marriage and sleeps with her, he must pay the full dowry for her to be his wife” (verse 16).

“If her father absolutely refuses to give her to him, the man still must pay an amount comparable to the bridal price of a virgin” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
This law assumes a custom called the bride-price, mohar in Hebrew: a payment from the groom to the bride's father that sealed a marriage. A man who slept with an unmarried woman had taken what belonged to a marriage, so he had to pay the full bride-price and marry her, if her father agreed.

The law makes the man answer for what he did. He cannot take what he wanted and walk away. And her father may refuse the marriage. The man still has to pay.

The law is written around the father and the payment, which can sound cold to a modern reader. It reflects a world where a daughter's marriage was arranged by her family. But its point is that the man who used her must bear the cost, and that she is not to be left with nothing.
passages.later:
Paul calls believers to honor one another's bodies: “each of you must know how to control his own body in holiness and honor” (1 Thessalonians 4:4), “and no one should ever violate or exploit his brother in this regard” (1 Thessalonians 4:6).

He also writes, “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18).
passages.hard:
Does this law force a woman to marry the man who used her?

The law gives the choice to her father, not to the man. The father may refuse, and the man must pay all the same. The law does not speak of what the woman herself wants, and a modern reader notices that. These laws were written for a world where families arranged marriages, and they aimed to protect a woman from being used and left with nothing.

These verses must never be used to press anyone into marrying a person who has harmed them.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law would not let a man take what he wanted and walk away. Ask whether you have treated anyone as someone to use and leave. And ask what it means to honor another person's body and future as God does.

passages.t: Sorcery, and two other capital laws
passages.happening:
“You must not allow a sorceress to live” (verse 18).

“Whoever lies with an animal must surely be put to death” (verse 19).

“If anyone sacrifices to any god other than the LORD alone, he must be set apart for destruction” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Here the voice of the law changes. The cases framed with ‘if’ stop, and short, absolute commands begin, much like the Ten Commandments.

These three laws belong together. Each treats a deep breach of Israel's covenant with God. Sorcery tried to gain power from other gods or spirits, outside the LORD's rule. In Israel, where God himself was king, it was treated as treason against him, beside sacrifice to other gods in verse 20. Lying with an animal broke the order of creation, the line between human beings and beasts. ‘Set apart for destruction’ translates one Hebrew word, herem, used of what was given over wholly to God, often for destruction.

These are grave laws, and they should be read soberly. They were laws for Israel under God's direct rule, judged by courts. They are not a pattern for anyone today.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy names the practices this law had in view: “Let no one be found among you who sacrifices his son or daughter in the fire, practices divination or conjury, interprets omens, practices sorcery” (Deuteronomy 18:10).

The New Testament still treats sorcery as sin, listing it among the works of the flesh: “idolatry and sorcery” (Galatians 5:20). But its answer is repentance. When people in Ephesus turned to Christ, “a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books and burned them in front of everyone” (Acts 19:19).
passages.hard:
Should the command against allowing a sorceress to live be applied today?

No. Few verses have done more harm in the church's history. In early modern Europe and in colonial America, including the Salem trials of 1692, this verse was cited to justify putting to death people accused of witchcraft. Most of them were women, and many were plainly innocent. That was a misuse of Scripture, and it was wrong. The witch trials also broke this law's own safeguards, which required credible witnesses and careful judgment before any sentence of death.

The law was given to Israel as a people under God's direct rule. Christians of nearly every tradition hold that the civil penalties of Israel's law do not carry over to modern states, though they explain this in different ways. The New Testament still calls sorcery sin, but its remedy is repentance, as at Ephesus, never a death sentence by a church or a crowd. No one may use this verse to accuse, harm or drive out any person.
passages.asks: The people of Ephesus burned their own books when they turned to Christ. Ask whether there is anything you rely on for power or safety instead of God. And ask how quickly you suspect others, and whether you would want to be judged with the same haste.

passages.t: The foreigner, the widow, the orphan, and the poor
passages.happening:
“You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (verse 21).

“You must not mistreat any widow or orphan. If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry” (verses 22-23). God's anger will burn, and the oppressors' own wives will be widows and their children fatherless (verse 24).

“If you lend money to one of My people among you who is poor, you must not act as a creditor to him; you are not to charge him interest” (verse 25).

“If you take your neighbor’s cloak as collateral, return it to him by sunset, because his cloak is the only covering he has for his body. What else will he sleep in? And if he cries out to Me, I will hear, for I am compassionate” (verses 26-27).
passages.hearers:
This is the heart of the chapter. God now speaks for himself: ‘I will surely hear’.

The foreign resident, the ger, was someone living among a people not his own, without land or clan to protect him. Israel had been exactly that in Egypt. So the law turns memory into duty. You know what it is to be a stranger. Do not do to others what was done to you.

The widow and the orphan had lost the husband or father who would have spoken for them. God names himself their defender. The people who once cried out in Egypt and were heard (2:23-24) are told that God will hear anyone they oppress. The threat in verse 24 is measure for measure: those who make widows and orphans will see their own wives widowed and their children fatherless. God takes the side of the weak even when the oppressor belongs to his own people.

Interest on loans was normal in the ancient world, and rates on grain could be steep. Israel was forbidden to charge interest to a poor fellow Israelite. A loan to someone in need was meant to lift him, not to profit from him.

The cloak law pictures the poorest borrower, whose outer garment was also his blanket. A lender could hold it by day as a pledge, but had to give it back by night. A letter written in ink on a broken piece of pottery, found at Mesad Hashavyahu on Israel's coast and dated to the late seventh century BC, records a field worker's plea for the return of his garment, taken by an overseer. It shows the kind of case this law had in view.

And the reason God gives is his own heart: ‘I am compassionate’. The Hebrew word is channun, gracious. It comes back in 34:6, when God proclaims his own name.
passages.later:
Leviticus goes further than ‘do not oppress’: “You must treat the foreigner living among you as native-born and love him as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 19:34). Deuteronomy says God “loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing” (Deuteronomy 10:18).

Jesus said, “I was a stranger and you took Me in” (Matthew 25:35), and told his followers to lend “expecting nothing in return” (Luke 6:35). James defines true religion this way: “to care for orphans and widows in their distress” (James 1:27).
passages.asks: God says he hears the cry of the person with only one cloak. Ask whose cry you may not be hearing: a stranger, a widow, a child without a parent, someone in debt. And ask what part of your own story, as a stranger or as one in need, should make you more merciful now.

passages.t: Reverence, firstfruits, and a holy people
passages.happening:
“You must not blaspheme God or curse the ruler of your people” (verse 28).

“You must not hold back offerings from your granaries or vats. You are to give Me the firstborn of your sons” (verse 29). Firstborn cattle and sheep stay with their mothers seven days, and on the eighth day are given to God (verse 30).

“You are to be My holy people. You must not eat the meat of a mauled animal found in the field; you are to throw it to the dogs” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends where Israel's life began: with God. The people are not to curse God or the leaders he set over them.

They are to bring the first of their harvest without delay. ‘Give Me the firstborn of your sons’ does not mean sacrifice. Israel's firstborn sons belonged to God because he spared them on the night of the Passover, and they were redeemed, bought back with an offering (13:13).

Then the purpose of all these laws: ‘You are to be My holy people’. Holiness reaches from the altar to the lending table and to the dinner plate. Meat torn by a wild animal in the field was not to be eaten; it was left for the dogs. Honoring God, caring for the poor and what a family eats all belong to one holy life.
passages.later:
Paul quoted verse 28 when he learned he had spoken sharply to the high priest: “for it is written: ‘Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people’” (Acts 23:5).

Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to the temple under this law, “as it is written in the Law of the Lord: ‘Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord’” (Luke 2:23).

Peter calls believers by the same name: “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9).
passages.asks: God's people were to bring him the first, not the leftovers. Ask what you give God first, and what you give him only after everything else. And ask how holiness might reach into the ordinary parts of your week.
